idiom_name: immutable record/value replacement published with one reference store (AtomicReference for shared state)
implementation_notes: Java cannot overload the assignment operator and has no user-defined value types, so the pattern's ordering is expressed by never mutating published state: a record (or a final-field class) builds a complete replacement -- including defensive copies of its mutable components in a compact constructor -- and the caller publishes it with a single reference assignment, while the garbage collector takes the destructor's role of releasing the old state. For state read by several threads, keep it behind one volatile or AtomicReference field and commit with set, getAndSet, updateAndGet or compareAndSet; that reference exchange is the closest Java has to the non-throwing swap. The hand-rolled form -- copy every field into a temporary, then copy it back into the live object -- is the shape to avoid: it is not atomic and concurrent readers can observe the half-updated object, while the immutable-replacement version cannot expose an intermediate state at all.
pitfalls: Records are shallow: without List.copyOf/Map.copyOf in the compact constructor the object shares the caller's mutable collection, and Collections.unmodifiableList is only a view that still changes when someone else mutates the backing list.

AtomicReference.set makes the store atomic but not the read-modify-write: two writers building from the same snapshot silently lose one update unless updateAndGet/compareAndSet is used, and the update function may be retried, so it must be side-effect-free.

Safe publication still requires final fields or a volatile/atomic reference: an object that escapes its constructor or writes non-final state afterwards can be seen half-built even if it is never mutated again.
A record used as a map key is only stable if every component it contributes to equals/hashCode is itself immutable -- sharing a mutable element makes the key change under the collection.
